passages.t: All Israel makes David king, and Jerusalem is taken
passages.happening:
‘Then all Israel came together to David at Hebron’ (verse 1). They say, “Here we are, your own flesh and blood” (verse 1). Even while Saul was king, David led Israel out and brought them back, and the LORD had said, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them’ (verse 2). So the elders come to Hebron, David makes a covenant with them before the LORD, ‘And they anointed him king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD through Samuel’ (verse 3).

David and all Israel march to Jerusalem, then called Jebus. The people there say, “You will never get in here” (verse 5). ‘Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David)’ (verse 5). Joab goes up first and becomes chief commander (verse 6). David builds up the city, ‘And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of Hosts was with him’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The Chronicler moves straight from Saul's death to all Israel at Hebron. He passes over the seven years when David ruled Judah alone while Saul's son ruled the north, and the civil war between them, which 2 Samuel tells. Here the whole nation comes at once, united, recognizing what God has said. Verses 1 to 9 follow 2 Samuel 5 closely.

Calling David their own flesh and blood was a claim of kinship, the ancient basis of loyalty. The covenant set out the relationship between king and people before the LORD. To anoint, mashach, was to set someone apart for a task by God; from it comes mashiach, anointed one, behind the word Messiah. The king's first task is to shepherd, raah: care for a flock that belongs to God.

Jerusalem was a Canaanite city on a narrow ridge with steep valleys on three sides and the Gihon spring at its foot, strong and easy to defend. It lay between Judah and the northern tribes and belonged to none of them, a neutral capital. David is usually dated about 1010 to 970 BC, and the capture of the city commonly around 1000 BC. The supporting terraces translate the Hebrew Millo. Archaeologists have uncovered a large stepped stone structure on the eastern slope of the City of David that some link with it, though its date and purpose are debated.
passages.later: Second Samuel gives the same words: ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them’ (2 Samuel 5:2). A psalm of David says, “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1). Ezekiel later promised ‘one shepherd, My servant David’ (Ezekiel 34:23).
passages.hard:
Why does Chronicles leave out the civil war, David's years ruling Judah alone, and other parts of Samuel's account?

The Chronicler leaves out David's seven years in Hebron as king of Judah only, his war with Saul's house, and later his adultery with Bathsheba and Absalom's revolt. Some critics have seen this as idealizing David or even whitewashing him. Most scholars now read it differently. The Chronicler's readers already had Samuel and Kings; he was not hiding what everyone knew. He chose and arranged his material to make his own points for his own generation: that David was the king God chose, that all Israel was united under him, and that his reign turned toward God's house. He even mentions the seven years in Hebron in passing (3:4; 29:27), and he includes Uriah the Hittite among the mighty men (verse 41), a name his readers would recognize. Chronicles is best read beside Samuel and Kings, as a second portrait from another angle, not as a replacement.
passages.asks: All Israel came and claimed David as their own flesh and blood. Ask what it would take for divided people around you to recognize what binds them. And ask whom you are called to shepherd, and whether you treat them as yours or as God's.

passages.t: The mighty men, and water from Bethlehem
passages.happening:
The chiefs of David's mighty men are named, who with all Israel ‘strengthened his kingdom’ (verse 10). Jashobeam and Eleazar stand first (verses 11-14).

Once, when the Philistines held Bethlehem, David longs for water and says, “Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!” (verse 17). Three of his men break through the Philistine camp and bring it back. ‘But he refused to drink it; instead, he poured it out to the LORD’ (verse 18), saying, “Far be it from me, my God, to do this! How can I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?” (verse 19).

Abishai and Benaiah's exploits follow (verses 20-25), and then a long roll of names (verses 26-47), among them ‘Uriah the Hittite’ (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
The mighty men were an elite corps, in ranks: the Three, the Thirty and their commanders. Second Samuel places their roll near the end of David's life; the Chronicler sets it at the beginning, to show that David's kingdom was built with a great company of loyal followers. The list through Uriah follows 2 Samuel 23, and the names after him come from another source. Several were foreigners, among them an Ammonite, a Moabite and Uriah the Hittite: loyalty to David could cross the lines between peoples.

David's pouring out of the water was a drink offering. In Israel's law blood belonged to God as the seat of life, and David treats water won at the risk of lives as if it were their blood, too precious to drink and fit only to be given to God.

The account of Eleazar seems to join the stories of two warriors, Eleazar and Shammah, told separately in 2 Samuel. Many scholars think a copyist's eye skipped from one mention of the Philistines gathering to the next and dropped the lines between.
passages.later: In 2 Samuel David says, “Far be it from me, O LORD, to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?” (2 Samuel 23:17).
passages.asks: David would not drink what had cost his men so much. Ask what sacrifices others have made for you that you have taken for granted. And ask what it would mean to give such gifts back to God rather than use them up on yourself.
